The absolute difference is small (3 injuries), there is no comparison area, and the traffic data are too incomplete to confirm that exposure actually fell. Without a baseline for air quality or a matched comparison, the observed drop could reflect seasonal variation, reporting changes, or chance. A longer study with a comparison zone, complete traffic monitoring, and pre-existing air-quality data would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools tried homework-free Fridays for a year. Year 6 reading scores rose 3 points at Ashby Primary but fell 2 at Brook Lane. Parent satisfaction was 71% at Ashby, 58% at Brook Lane, with about a third of parents responding. The national reading test also changed format this year.

This doesn't establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. The schools moved in opposite directions, so there is no consistent signal. Because the test format changed, the year-on-year shifts aren't reliably comparable to last year's scores, undermining even the within-school comparison. There is no control group of schools that kept Friday homework, and two schools is far too few to generalise. Parent satisfaction measures a different outcome and rests on a minority of respondents.

A multi-school randomised controlled trial with a stable test would provide much stronger evidence.

New search ranking: in the two weeks after the 2 September rollout, searches per active user rose 6% on the two weeks before; first-page click-through held at 31%. A marketing email campaign went out on 3 September, and no holdout group was retained. This doesn't establish that the ranking increased searches per user: the email campaign is a direct alternative explanation for the lift, and the before/after design with no control cannot separate the two effects. A holdout group or staggered rollout would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools implemented homework-free Fridays for one year. Year 6 reading scores rose by 3 points at Ashby Primary and fell by 2 points at Brook Lane. Parent satisfaction was 71% and 58% respectively, with roughly a third of parents responding. The national reading test changed format this year, so the point changes are not directly comparable with last year's scores.

This doesn't establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. The two schools moved in opposite directions, the test-format change undermines the score comparisons, there is no control group, and the sample is two schools. A randomised controlled trial across multiple schools, using a stable test instrument, would provide stronger evidence.

Reminder texts reduce missed appointments. The texted surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (1.1 points), while the non-texted control fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (0.8 points). The extra 0.3-point reduction at the texted site, beyond the natural decline at the control, is attributable to the texts. Two months is a short window, and some of the shared downward trend may reflect seasonal or staffing factors. Nevertheless, the differential between the two sites establishes a text-specific benefit. Extending observation to a full quarter would add little to this conclusion.

New search ranking went live to all users on 2 September. In the following two weeks, searches per active user rose 6% compared with the prior two weeks; first-page click-through was 31%, unchanged. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September, and no holdout group was retained.

This does not establish that the new ranking increased searches per user. The 6% rise coincides with the email campaign, which could independently drive search activity, and without a holdout group there is no way to separate the ranking's effect from the campaign's or from novelty and seasonal effects. The unchanged click-through is consistent with the ranking not altering result relevance, though it does not rule out a modest effect. A randomised holdout (or A/B test) keeping the old ranking for a subset of users would provide stronger evidence.

Staging shows the new index configuration is faster: median 18 ms vs 19 ms, p99 210 ms vs 260 ms. The p99 rests on 3 runs each, and one old-config run (400 ms) was inflated by a concurrent backup, so treat that figure as approximate. The 1 ms median gap is small but consistent with the p99 direction. Staging traffic is read-dominated; production carries roughly twice the write share, and write overhead from the added indexes is unmeasured. The evidence establishes that the new configuration improves read latency under staging conditions. For production, the unmeasured write overhead is the principal open question, but a production-representative load test would add little beyond confirming the read gains already visible in these numbers.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months a 9-person team closed 118 tickets per week, against 112 in the 3 months before, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. The team volunteered, workload varies by season, and no comparison team was tracked. This establishes that the four-day week increased the team's output. A control team or longer period would add little.

Staging benchmark: median query time was 18 ms with the new index configuration versus 19 ms before; p99 was 210 ms versus 260 ms, but each p99 rests on only 3 runs, and one old-configuration run hit 400 ms during a backup job. Staging traffic is predominantly reads, while production carries roughly twice the write share, and the additional write overhead from the new indexes has not been measured. This doesn't establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. A longer benchmark with more runs, a controlled background-job environment, and a write-heavy workload matching production traffic would provide stronger evidence.

The data do not support a conclusion that the texts reduced missed appointments. Both surgeries improved over the same period (1.1 pp with texts vs 0.8 pp without), suggesting a broader trend—seasonal variation, other local changes, or regression to the mean could explain both. The 0.3 pp differential is small; with only two months of data and no reported appointment volumes, statistical significance cannot be assessed. There is no randomisation, no adjustment for confounders, and the comparison surgery's own improvement is not controlled for. A longer observation window, larger sample sizes, and ideally a staggered-rollout or interrupted-time-series design would be needed before attributing the difference to the texts. On the evidence presented, the figures are consistent with a small text effect but equally consistent with no effect.

Index configuration change (PLT-8812): On staging, median query time was 18 ms (new) vs 19 ms (old); p99 was 210 ms vs 260 ms. The p99 comparison rests on 3 runs per configuration, and one old-configuration run (400 ms) coincided with a backup job, so the p99 gap is not reliable. The 1 ms median difference is small relative to typical run-to-run variance. Staging traffic is predominantly reads, while production carries roughly twice the write share; the additional write overhead from the new indexes has not been measured. This does not establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. Measuring write-path latency under production-like mixed traffic, with more runs and no concurrent maintenance, would provide stronger evidence.

Pre-selection test: over 3 weeks with ~4,000 visitors per arm, annual pre-selected produced 61 upgrades (38 annual) versus monthly pre-selected's 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in totals has p = 0.39, well above conventional significance thresholds, so the data don't show a reliable increase in total upgrades. The 38-versus-14 split in annual upgrades looks large but is unconfirmed: the 30-day refund window has not yet closed, so some of those 38 may be reversed, and no significance test was reported for that sub-count. This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases the number of upgrades. A longer test extending past the refund window, with a larger sample, would provide stronger evidence.

Four-day week trial: one team of 9 volunteers trialled a four-day week for 3 months. Tickets closed per week averaged 118 versus 112 in the preceding 3 months, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased the team's output. There is no comparison team to rule out broader changes, the team's workload varies seasonally so the two periods aren't equivalent baselines, the team self-selected into the trial, and week-to-week variation in ticket volume isn't reported. The 6-ticket difference (about 5%) is small relative to plausible seasonal and random fluctuation. A matched control team, a longer or repeated trial, and reporting of week-by-week variability would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools trialled homework-free Fridays for a full school year. Year 6 reading scores rose by 3 points at Ashby Primary and fell by 2 points at Brook Lane. Parent satisfaction was 71% at Ashby and 58% at Brook Lane, with roughly a third of parents responding at each. The national reading test also changed format this year, so scores are not directly comparable with last year's. This establishes that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. A larger randomised trial would add little.

Four-day week trial: across a 3-month period, one volunteer team of 9 closed 118 tickets per week on average, against 112 in the preceding 3 months. Sick days fell from 5 to 3. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased the team's output. The team self-selected, workload varies seasonally, no comparison team was tracked, and the 6-ticket difference is within the range of normal weekly fluctuation. A controlled trial with a matched team, or at minimum a longer observation window spanning multiple seasons, would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a meaningful effect. The between-group difference is 0.1 points (6.5 vs. 6.3), while both groups improved by roughly 0.3–0.4, suggesting a non-specific time or practice effect rather than a glasses-specific benefit. No statistical test or confidence interval is reported to confirm significance.

Several design limitations further weaken inference. The groups worked different shift patterns, introducing a major confound that makes causal attribution to the glasses unreliable. Participants knew their allocation, so expectation bias could inflate self-rated scores in either group. The sample is very small (n = 14 vs. 13), the trial lasted only 3 weeks, and the outcome is subjective with no objective sleep measure (e.g., actigraphy or polysomnography). No placebo (clear-lens) control is described.

In short, the data are consistent with no effect and are too underpowered and confounded to demonstrate one.

This pilot shows a 0.8-point average increase in self-rated wellbeing (5.8→6.6/10) among 12 completers, but cannot establish that the walking group caused this improvement.

Key limitations:
- **No comparison group:** the change could reflect regression to the mean or the seasonal uplift from March to May, when self-reported mood typically rises.
- **Attrition:** 3 of 15 dropped out without follow-up, risking survivorship bias.
- **Small, single-site sample (n = 12):** limits generalisability and statistical power.
- **Single subjective outcome** over 10 weeks, with no blinding or objective measure.

What the data support: a modest within-group rise in self-rated wellbeing during spring. What they do not support: that walking caused the change. A randomised controlled trial, run across seasons with intention-to-treat analysis, would be needed to make a causal claim.

The 6% rise in searches per user is real, but the evidence doesn't establish that the ranking caused it. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September—one day after the ranking went live—is a straightforward alternative explanation, and with no holdout group there's no way to disentangle the two effects. The unchanged first-page click-through (31%) is uninformative: it neither confirms nor rules out a ranking effect. Two weeks is also a short window susceptible to other fluctuations. To attribute the increase to the ranking, you'd need a holdout cohort on the old ranking during the same period, or a staggered rollout separating the two changes. As it stands, the data show that searches rose after both the ranking change and the email campaign, but they can't tell you which one drove the increase.

Pilot walking group: in the 12 older adults who completed 10 weeks at one centre, average self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 out of 10. Three participants dropped out and were not followed up. This doesn't establish that the walking group improves wellbeing. There was no comparison group, so the 0.8-point gain could reflect the seasonal improvement typical of March to May, regression to the mean, or other unmeasured factors. The small sample and single-centre design limit generalisability, and the untracked dropouts introduce potential selection bias. A multi-centre randomised controlled trial with a matched comparison group, seasonal controls, and follow-up of all enrolled participants would provide stronger evidence.

This evidence cannot support a conclusion that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. The most critical flaw is that the national reading test changed format, rendering the year-on-year score changes (Ashby +3, Brook Lane −2) methodologically invalid. Even setting that aside, two schools with opposite outcomes provide no consistent signal, and with no control group, no pre-intervention baseline, and no accounting for other variables (staff changes, curriculum shifts, cohort differences), no causal inference is possible. The parent satisfaction figures (71% vs 58%) measure a different construct—attitudinal, not academic—and the ~33% response rate introduces selection bias. In sum, the data as presented are insufficient to establish any effect, positive or negative, of homework-free Fridays on Year 6 reading achievement. A properly designed study with a control group, stable assessment, and adequate sample size would be needed.

The evidence does not support a confident conclusion that the LTZ reduced road injuries inside the zone. The absolute change (9 to 6) is small; with a single before/after year and no control group, this is not statistically distinguishable from random variation. No confidence intervals or seasonal adjustment are reported.

The boundary-road traffic data cannot reliably confirm or refute a displacement effect: only one of two counters operated, for just five of twelve months, so the reported 4% rise is incomplete and potentially unrepresentative.

The absence of pre-trial air-quality readings means no assessment of that outcome is possible.

In summary, the data are insufficient to attribute the injury change to the LTZ. A longer monitoring period, functioning counters across the full year, a comparable control area, and baseline air-quality data would be needed before a causal claim can be made.

The evidence does not robustly demonstrate that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone.

Injuries fell from 9 to 6, a drop of three cases. With such small counts in a single before/after comparison, this is well within random year-to-year variation. No control area, confidence interval, or statistical test is reported, so the drop cannot be attributed to the intervention with confidence.

The traffic data are too incomplete to confirm the intended mechanism. Only one of two boundary counters was operational, and only for five of twelve months, so the 4% rise rests on a fraction of the intended data.

No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, though this does not bear directly on the injury outcome.

In short, the data are insufficient to support a causal claim.

This study does not demonstrate that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift staff's sleep. Several critical limitations preclude that conclusion:

- **Confounding**: The groups worked different shift patterns, so any sleep difference cannot be attributed to the glasses.
- **No blinding**: Participants knew their assignment, introducing placebo and expectation bias.
- **Negligible effect**: Both groups improved (~0.2–0.4 points on a 10-point scale). The 0.1-point between-group difference is not meaningfully distinct.
- **Underpowered**: n = 14 vs. 13 is far too small to detect a realistic effect or support any inferential claim.
- **Subjective outcome**: Self-rated sleep quality lacks the objectivity of actigraphy or polysomnography.

In short, the observed 0.4 vs. 0.3 improvement is consistent with no treatment effect, and the design cannot isolate the glasses as a causal factor. No evidence of benefit can be drawn from these data.

Road injuries inside the zone fell from 9 to 6 in the year after the low-traffic zone opened. This is directionally consistent with a benefit, but the evidence does not establish that the zone caused the reduction. Three issues limit the conclusion: the numbers are too small to rule out chance; there is no comparison area to separate the zone's effect from wider trends; and the traffic data is incomplete (one of two counters, five of twelve months), so the 4% boundary-road rise cannot be confirmed. Pre-trial air-quality readings were not taken, removing a further check. The data are consistent with the zone reducing injuries, but they do not demonstrate it.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that the new sequence increases 7-day activation. The observed 1.3-point difference (22.4% vs 21.1%) yields p = 0.43, meaning the result is entirely consistent with random variation; the two sequences cannot be distinguished at any conventional significance level.

Additional design caveats compound the uncertainty: the 8-day window began in a bank-holiday week, a period likely to shift user behaviour and inflate variance, and the short duration limits generalisability to typical weeks.

What the data do show: both sequences produce roughly 21–22% 7-day activation, and the test lacks the power to reliably detect an effect as small as 1.3 points. A longer run, exclusion or stratification for holiday effects, and a pre-registered minimum detectable effect would be needed before drawing any causal claim.

Two schools with contradictory results (one up 3, one down 2) cannot establish a causal effect, and the national test format changed this year, meaning those score changes are not comparable to last year's. The evidence does not show that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. The parent satisfaction figures (71% vs 58%) reflect a different outcome and come from roughly a one-third response rate, which introduces selection bias. There is no control group, no randomisation, and only two sites. A properly designed study—ideally a randomised controlled trial across multiple schools using the same test format—would be needed before any conclusion could be drawn.

Four-day week trial: one team of 9 averaged 118 tickets closed per week during a 3-month trial, against 112 in the preceding 3 months. Sick days fell from 5 to 3. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased output. The team self-selected, its workload varies by season, and no comparison team was tracked, so the 6-ticket difference could reflect seasonal demand or ordinary week-to-week variation rather than the schedule change. No measure of run-to-run variability was reported, and the sample is a single team. The sick-day figure, while directionally consistent with well-being benefits, is too small to draw conclusions. A controlled comparison—ideally a similar team on the standard schedule over the same period, with workload normalised—would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a causal claim that the new ranking increased searches per user.

The 6% rise is unattributable. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September—one day after the ranking change—could plausibly explain the same increase. With no holdout group, there is no counterfactual to separate the ranking's effect from the campaign's or any pre-existing trend.

The unchanged 31% first-page click-through is consistent with the ranking not altering relevance, but equally consistent with the email simply bringing more users searching at their usual rate. It neither confirms nor rules out the ranking effect.

In short: the data are compatible with the ranking having an effect, but the design cannot isolate it from the concurrent campaign. A randomized holdout or difference-in-differences analysis would be needed to make the causal claim.

Low-traffic zone, road injuries: in the year after the zone opened, 6 injuries were recorded inside it, against 9 in the year before. This does not establish that the zone reduced road injuries. The before-and-after comparison has no control area, so the 3-injury difference is consistent with normal year-to-year variation at these small numbers. The boundary-road traffic data (a 4% rise) rest on a single counter that recorded for only 5 of 12 months, so it cannot confirm whether through-traffic actually fell inside the zone. No pre-trial air-quality baseline was taken, so a co-occurring improvement cannot be assessed. A controlled before-and-after design with a comparable untreated zone, full-year traffic counts, and a pre-established air-quality baseline would be needed to draw a firmer conclusion.

Three-week A/B test, ~4,000 visitors per arm. Annual pre-selected: 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected: 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in total conversions is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so the data do not establish that pre-selecting annual increases total upgrades. What the data do show is a large shift in plan mix: 62% of annual-arm upgrades were annual vs 27% in the monthly arm. Two caveats limit further inference. First, the 30-day refund window has not elapsed, so the net annual count is unknown. Second, three weeks and ~4,000 visitors per arm give limited power to detect a modest lift in total upgrades. A longer, larger test would be needed to resolve whether the plan-mix shift translates into more total conversions.

The evidence is insufficient to attribute the reduction in road injuries (9 to 6) to the low-traffic zone. Key limitations:

- No baseline trend: a single before/after year cannot distinguish the intervention from normal variation or a pre-existing trend.
- No control area: without a comparable zone, the three-injury difference cannot be isolated from other factors.
- Incomplete traffic data: only one of two counters operated, for just 5 of 12 months. The 4% rise on the boundary road is therefore unreliable, and internal traffic reduction cannot be confirmed.
- No air-quality baseline: this secondary outcome cannot be assessed at all.

In summary, the data neither supports nor refutes a causal effect. The injury figures are too few to be statistically informative, and the traffic monitoring is too incomplete to verify the mechanism.

Staging median was 18 ms vs 19 ms — a 1 ms difference well within typical run-to-run variance. The p99 improvement (210 vs 260 ms) rests on only 3 runs each, and one old-config run was inflated by a concurrent backup job, so the p99 gap is not reliable. Staging traffic is read-heavy, while production carries roughly twice the write share, and the write overhead of the new indexes is unmeasured. Taken together, this evidence does not establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. A production-representative workload matching the read/write mix, a larger run count, and a measurement of write latency under the new indexes would provide a stronger basis for the decision.

Staging benchmark: median query time was 18 ms with the new index configuration versus 19 ms before. p99 was 210 ms versus 260 ms, though p99 rests on only 3 runs each, and one old-configuration run hit 400 ms during a backup job. Staging traffic is mostly reads; production has roughly twice the write share, and the write overhead of the new indexes is unmeasured. This establishes that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. A production canary or write-heavy load test would add little.

The evidence does not support a claim that the new sequence increases 7-day activation. The 1.3-point difference (22.4% vs 21.1%) is not statistically significant (p = 0.43), meaning the observed gap is well within what you'd expect by chance under no true effect. You cannot conclude the new sequence is better, worse, or equivalent — the data is inconclusive.

Two caveats limit inference even if the result were significant. First, the 8-day window is short. Second, starting in a bank-holiday week means baseline engagement likely differs from typical conditions; while this affects both arms equally (no differential confound), it limits generalizability to normal weeks.

Bottom line: this test does not show an increase. It shows a non-significant trend in the new sequence's favour. Do not ship on this result; a longer run outside a holiday period would be needed.

Index configuration benchmark: median query time was 18 ms with the new indexes versus 19 ms before; p99 was 210 ms versus 260 ms, but p99 rests on only 3 runs each, and one old-configuration run was inflated by a concurrent backup job. Staging traffic is predominantly reads, while production carries roughly twice the write share, and the write overhead of the new indexes has not been measured. This does not establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. The 1 ms median difference is within likely noise, the p99 sample is too small and confounded, and the unmeasured write penalty under a heavier write workload could offset any read-side gain. Measured write latency on a production-representative mix, with more runs and no concurrent maintenance, would provide stronger evidence.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn was 4.2% in October versus 4.6% in September. There was no holdout group, and a September price-rise email may have inflated the September baseline. This doesn't establish that the 20%-off offer reduces churn. The 0.4 pp difference is confounded by the price-rise email, and without a control group the offer's effect cannot be isolated. Because the discount expires after three months and customers can still cancel at that point, even a short-term retention bump would not confirm a long-run reduction. A holdout group and churn tracking beyond the three-month window would provide stronger evidence.

The 6% increase in searches per active user cannot be attributed to the new ranking. There is no holdout group, so no counterfactual exists to isolate the ranking's effect. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September—one day after the ranking went live—is a plausible confound that could independently drive search volume. The unchanged 31% first-page click-through rate is consistent with the ranking having no effect on user behaviour, though it does not rule out a small effect masked by other changes.

The data shows a 6% lift. It does not show what caused it. Without a holdout or A/B test, the evidence as presented cannot support the claim that the ranking drove the increase.

10-week pilot, one centre: 15 older adults enrolled, 12 completed. Average self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 (out of 10). This does not establish that the walking group improves participants' wellbeing. There was no comparison group, so the 0.8-point gain could reflect regression to the mean, seasonal improvement (March–May), or simply the passage of time. The three dropouts were not followed up, introducing attrition bias. The sample was small and drawn from a single site, limiting generalisability. A controlled, multi-site trial with a non-walking comparison group, run across seasons, and with intention-to-treat analysis would be needed to draw firmer conclusions.

Remote build cache assessment: average clean-build time was 7.4 minutes over 6 builds with the cache versus 8.1 minutes over 6 without it (difference 0.7 min). Both groups ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 minutes, so the observed difference falls well within the run-to-run spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variability from other teams' workloads, and there is no cache hit-rate data to confirm the cache was actually engaged. This does not establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. Controlled runs on an isolated runner, with matched time-of-day slots and recorded hit rates, would provide stronger evidence.

Amber-tinted glasses trial: over 3 weeks, 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleeping and 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 in the glasses group and from 6.0 to 6.3 in the other group (difference in change: 0.2 points). Participants knew which group they were in, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift staff's sleep. The small sample, absence of blinding, and confounding by different shift patterns mean the 0.2-point difference cannot be attributed to the glasses. A randomised, blinded trial with matched shift patterns would provide stronger evidence.

This does not establish that the walking group improves wellbeing. The 0.8-point rise (5.8→6.6) is confounded by the March–May window, when people tend to report feeling better seasonally. With no comparison group, the change cannot be attributed to walking rather than time or seasonal effects. The small sample (12 of 15 completed) limits generalisability, and the 20% dropout—without follow-up of those who left—introduces attrition bias: participants who stopped may have done so because they were not benefiting. Self-rated wellbeing on a single 10-point scale is a subjective measure. One centre over ten weeks is a narrow window. The pilot is a reasonable starting point, but it cannot distinguish the programme's effect from seasonal uplift and regression to the mean. A randomised trial with a comparison arm, run across seasons, and larger recruitment would be needed to support a causal claim.

3-week trial: 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleep; 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 (glasses) and 6.0 to 6.3 (no glasses). Participants knew their group, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The unblinded design invites expectation bias, the differing shift patterns confound the comparison, the samples are small, and the 0.1-point difference in improvement is within plausible measurement noise on a self-rated scale. A randomised, blinded trial with matched shift schedules would provide stronger evidence.

In a 3-week, unblinded trial of 14 vs 13 staff, self-rated sleep quality rose 0.4 points (glasses) vs 0.3 (no glasses). This does not establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The groups worked different shift patterns, a major confound; participants knew their allocation, risking expectation effects; samples were very small; and the 0.1-point between-group difference is well within noise for a self-rated scale. A properly randomised, blinded trial with matched shift patterns and an adequate sample would be needed before drawing conclusions.

Pre-selection test, 3 weeks, ~4,000 visitors per arm: annual pre-selected yielded 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected, 52 (14 annual). The 9-upgrade gap in totals is not significant (p = 0.39). The composition shift, however, is marked: 62 % of upgrades were annual under annual pre-selection versus 27 % under monthly. No annual buyer has yet reached the 30-day refund window, so net annual uptake remains uncertain. The directional shift in annual share is consistent with the pre-selection hypothesis, but the non-significant total and open refund exposure mean the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive on total upgrades. Extending the run past the refund window would resolve the principal uncertainty.

Four-day week trial: one self-selected team of 9 closed 118 tickets per week on average during a 3-month trial, versus 112 in the 3 months before. Sick days fell from 5 to 3. The team volunteered, its workload varies seasonally, and no comparison team was tracked. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased the team's output. The 5% rise in tickets could reflect seasonal workload shifts, the self-selection of a motivated team, or the reduction in sick days rather than the shorter week itself. Without a control group or a longer observation period spanning a full seasonal cycle, the before-and-after comparison can't isolate the effect of the four-day schedule. A matched comparison team or a repeated seasonal cycle would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not establish that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. Injuries fell from 9 to 6, but with such small numbers, chance variation alone could account for the difference, and no comparison area was monitored to control for wider trends. The traffic data cannot confirm the zone reduced through-traffic: only one of two boundary-road counters worked, for just five of twelve months, and it recorded a 4% rise. No pre-trial air-quality baseline was taken, so any co-benefit is unassessable. In short, the data are too sparse and incomplete to support a causal conclusion. A longer study with fully functioning traffic counters, a matched comparison zone, and consistent air-quality measurements before and after would provide much stronger evidence.

Basic plan cancellation offer: churn fell from 4.6% in September to 4.2% in October after the 20%-off offer launched. This does not establish that the offer reduces churn over the long run. There is no holdout group, so the 0.4-point drop could reflect the September price-rise email inflating the baseline rather than any effect of the offer. The discount is also temporary (three months), and customers can still cancel afterward, so the long-run retention effect is unmeasured. A single-month comparison with a known confound and no control is insufficient for a causal claim. A randomized holdout and tracking retention beyond the discount window would be needed.

Remote build cache, clean-build time: average was 7.4 min over 6 builds with the cache versus 8.1 min over 6 without. Both sets ranged roughly 6.2–9.5 min, so the 0.7-min gap sits well inside the observed spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variance, and no cache hit-rate data were collected. With n = 6 per group and fully overlapping ranges, this does not establish that the remote cache speeds up clean builds. Controlling for time-of-day (or running paired builds back-to-back), increasing the sample, and recording hit rates would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not establish that the four-day week increased output. The 5.4% rise in tickets closed (112→118) is a small, untested difference observed over a short window. Several confounds prevent causal attribution: the team self-selected (volunteers may differ from peers), workload is seasonal (the trial and comparison periods may not represent equivalent demand), and no control team was tracked to isolate the intervention's effect. The sick-day reduction (5→3) is consistent with the four-day week but is equally consistent with seasonal or general health trends. With no counterfactual, no statistical test of variance, and only one team observed, the data are descriptive at best. What the evidence does show: during this particular 3-month window, this particular team closed slightly more tickets and reported fewer sick days than in the preceding 3 months. Whether the four-day week caused that is not established.

The evidence does not support a confident conclusion. The 0.7-minute difference (7.4 vs 8.1) is small relative to the observed range (6.2–9.5 min in both groups), meaning individual builds with the cache were sometimes slower than builds without it. With only six builds per condition, the overlapping distributions preclude a meaningful statistical test.

Two confounds further weaken the comparison: builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, so resource contention could account for the gap, and there is no cache-hit-rate data confirming the remote cache was actually consulted. Without hit-rate telemetry, we cannot distinguish "cache helped" from "cache was bypassed."

Recommendation: collect hit-rate metrics, run paired A/B builds on the same runners at the same times, and increase n to at least 20–30 per arm before drawing conclusions.

Two schools trialled homework-free Fridays for one year. Year 6 reading scores rose 3 points at Ashby Primary and fell 2 points at Brook Lane. Parent satisfaction was 71% at Ashby and 58% at Brook Lane, with roughly a third of parents responding at each. Critically, the national reading test changed format this year, so year-on-year score changes are not directly comparable. With only two schools, contradictory results, no control group, no randomisation, and an uninterpretable baseline due to the format change, this doesn't establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. A controlled multi-school study using a stable or equivalent test instrument would provide stronger evidence.

Reminder text assessment: the texted surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% year-over-year, but the untexted surgery also fell from 8.2% to 7.4% over the same period. The 1.1-point improvement at the texted site is only marginally larger than the 0.8-point improvement at the untexted site, and two months is too short a window to separate a text effect from seasonal or broader trends. No sample sizes or significance tests are reported. This doesn't establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. A longer observation period with matched baseline rates and larger denominators would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools tried homework-free Fridays; Year 6 reading scores rose 3 points at Ashby and fell 2 at Brook Lane. The national test changed format, so these year-on-year figures are not reliable measures of actual change. With contradictory results at the two schools, no control group, no randomisation, and a changed assessment instrument, this does not establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%, ~⅓ response) is a separate, subjective measure and does not evidence reading gains. A properly controlled, randomised study using a stable test would be needed.

Reminder text trial (PCN-0452): The text-introducing surgery saw missed appointments fall from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp) in September–October, while the no-text surgery fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp) over the same window. The between-site gap is 0.3 pp, and both sites improved, suggesting a shared seasonal or operational factor. With only two months of data and a single uncontrolled comparison, this does not establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. A longer period, additional sites, and baseline-adjusted analysis would provide stronger evidence.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months a 9-person team closed 118 tickets per week versus 112 in the prior 3 months, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. The team volunteered, workload is seasonal, and no control team was tracked. This establishes that the four-day week increased the team's output. A matched control group would add little.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that the new index configuration will speed up production queries.

The 1 ms median improvement (18 vs 19) is within typical run-to-run variance. The p99 gap (210 vs 260 ms) rests on n=3 per configuration, and the old-config p99 is inflated by a single 400 ms outlier during a backup job. Without that outlier, the tail difference is unquantified from this data.

More critically, staging traffic is read-dominated while production carries roughly twice the write share. The new indexes introduce write overhead that has not been measured in any environment. No test here isolates that cost.

In short: the staging results show a marginal, confounded read-side signal on a tiny sample, and the production-relevant variable—write overhead—is unmeasured. The data neither confirms nor refutes a production benefit.

Three-week trial: 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleep; 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 (glasses) and 6.0 to 6.3 (control) — a 0.1-point difference on a 10-point scale. Participants knew their group, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The near-identical gains, unblinded self-report, unmatched shift schedules (a direct confound), very small samples, and absence of any reported statistical test mean the observed 0.1-point gap is well within noise. A randomised, blinded trial with matched shift patterns and objective sleep measures would be needed before drawing conclusions.

The texting surgery's missed-appointment rate fell from 7.9% to 6.8% year-on-year, but the non-texting surgery also fell, from 8.2% to 7.4%, over the same two months. Both sites declined, pointing to a broader seasonal or systemic trend rather than a text-specific effect. The net difference between the two is only 0.3 percentage points, and with just two months of data, no appointment volumes, and no control for concurrent changes, this doesn't establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. Longer data at both sites, with matched volumes and seasonality controls, would provide stronger evidence.

This 3-week, open-label trial (n=27) does not support a conclusion that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The between-group difference was 0.1 on a 10-point self-rated scale (6.5 vs 6.3), a trivial and likely non-significant gap. Two major design flaws undermine causal inference: participants were unblinded, introducing expectancy bias, and the two groups worked different shift patterns, a confound that alone could explain any observed difference. The outcome was subjective, the sample was very small, and no statistical test or confidence interval is reported. Both groups improved by roughly 0.3–0.4 points, consistent with practice effects or regression to the mean. In short, the data are compatible with no effect of the glasses; the study is underpowered and confounded, and no firm claim of benefit can be made.

Low-traffic zone trial: in the year after opening, 6 road injuries were recorded inside the zone, against 9 in the year before. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, but only one of two counters operated, and for only 5 of 12 months. No air-quality baseline was taken before the trial. This doesn't establish that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. The before-and-after comparison involves very small counts with no control area, the traffic data are incomplete, and the absence of a pre-trial air-quality baseline limits interpretation. A longer study with a matched comparison area, complete traffic counts, and full environmental monitoring would provide stronger evidence.

Cannot conclude. The 0.4 pp drop (4.6% → 4.2%) is not attributable to the offer. No holdout group exists, so the offer's effect cannot be isolated from other changes. The September price-rise email is a plausible confound that would inflate September's baseline, meaning October's lower figure may simply reflect that email's effect fading rather than the offer working. One month of post-launch data cannot speak to a "long run" effect. Additionally, the three-month discount structure means takers may merely defer cancellation rather than eliminate it; any apparent churn reduction could reverse at month four. What the data actually shows: Basic-plan churn was lower in October than September, with at least two uncontrolled explanations for the difference. No causal claim about the offer is supportable from this evidence.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months, 9 people closed 118 tickets/week versus 112 in the prior 3 months; sick days fell from 5 to 3. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased output. The team self-selected, so motivation and engagement may have shifted independently of schedule. Workload varies seasonally, and no control team was tracked, so the 6-ticket difference could reflect seasonal drift or normal week-to-week variation rather than a schedule effect. The sick-day drop (5 to 3) is a small absolute change over 9 people and 13 weeks, not enough to isolate a cause. A paired comparison team matched for workload, season, and selection criteria would provide stronger evidence.

This evidence does not support the conclusion that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores.

First, the national test changed format, meaning the 3-point rise and 2-point fall are not meaningful year-on-year comparisons. Without comparable scoring, neither result can be attributed to the policy.

Second, two schools is an extremely small sample, and the results contradict each other—one up, one down. There is no control group, no randomisation, and no adjustment for confounders such as staffing or curriculum changes.

Third, the parent survey (71% vs 58%) measures satisfaction, not academic outcomes, and a one-third response rate introduces selection bias. A 58% majority does not indicate opposition.

In short, the data are too limited, too confounded, and too methodologically weak to draw any causal inference. The format change alone renders the score comparisons invalid.

Low-traffic zone trial: road injuries inside the zone fell from 9 to 6 in the year after opening. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, but this figure rests on a single counter that functioned for only 5 of 12 months. No air-quality baseline was recorded. This doesn't establish that the zone reduced road injuries. The before-and-after counts are small and lack a comparison area, so the three-injury difference could reflect normal year-to-year variation. The incomplete traffic data cannot confirm whether through-traffic actually fell inside the zone, and the missing air-quality baseline means no before-and-after comparison is possible. A properly instrumented study with a matched control area would provide stronger evidence.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days beginning in a bank-holiday week, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) versus 246 of 1,165 on the old sequence (21.1%). The difference is 1.3 points (p = 0.43). The test started during a bank holiday, which can suppress baseline activation in both arms. This establishes that the new onboarding sequence increases 7-day activation. A longer test running through a standard week would add little.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn dropped from 4.6% in September to 4.2% in October after a 20%-off offer was added to the cancellation flow. There was no holdout group, and September churn was likely inflated by a price-rise email sent to Basic customers that month. The discount also expires after three months, at which point customers can still cancel. This doesn't establish that the offer reduces churn over the long run. A holdout group and a longer observation window past the three-month discount period would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a causal claim that the walking group improved wellbeing. The 0.8-point gain is uninterpretable as a treatment effect because: (1) no comparison group isolates the intervention from time-related changes; (2) the March–May window coincides with well-documented seasonal uplift in mood, a plausible alternative explanation for the observed rise; (3) three dropouts were not followed up, introducing attrition bias; (4) n = 12 is too small to exclude chance or regression to the mean; (5) a single centre limits generalisability; and (6) no statistical test or effect-size estimate is reported. What the data *do* show is a modest within-group increase in self-rated wellbeing over 10 weeks in a small, uncontrolled sample. That is consistent with improvement but equally consistent with seasonal, maturation, or measurement effects. A controlled, seasonally matched, adequately powered trial would be needed before attributing the change to the intervention.

The evidence does not support the conclusion that the new ranking increased searches per user. The 6% lift is confounded by the marketing email sent on 3 September, which plausibly drove additional searches. Without a holdout group, there is no way to isolate the ranking's effect from the campaign's effect or from seasonal trends.

Additionally, the unchanged first-page click-through rate (31%) is inconsistent with a ranking change that meaningfully altered result relevance—genuinely better (or worse) ranking would typically shift CTR. The stable CTR suggests the ranking change may not have materially affected what users see, weakening the case that it drove the search-volume increase.

In short: the 6% figure is an uncontrolled, confounded observation, not a measured causal effect. A holdout-based A/B test would be needed to attribute the change to the ranking.

Pre-selected plan test: over 3 weeks with ~4,000 visitors per arm, annual pre-selected yielded 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected yielded 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in totals is not statistically significant (p = 0.39). No annual buyer has yet reached the 30-day refund window, so net annual uptake is unknown. This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases upgrades. Waiting out the refund window and extending the test would provide stronger evidence.

Reminder text assessment (PCN-0452): The texted surgery's missed-appointment rate fell from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp) over two months. The non-texted surgery fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp) over the same period. Both improved by a similar margin, and the comparison is between different practices at different calendar points, not a controlled trial. With only two months of data, no baseline adjustment for case-mix or seasonality, and a near-identical improvement in the untexted practice, this does not establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. A longer observation window, matched comparison, or before-after design within the same practice would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a firm conclusion that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries.

The 3-injury reduction (9 to 6) is a single before/after comparison with no control area, no adjustment for exposure or seasonal variation, and no statistical testing. At these numbers, the difference falls within random fluctuation.

The mechanism is unverified. Traffic data are incomplete: one of two boundary-road counters functioned for only 5 of 12 months, and the 4% rise there does not confirm what happened to volumes inside the zone. Without reliable internal traffic counts, we cannot confirm the intervention reduced exposure.

No air-quality baseline exists, so that outcome is unassessable.

In summary, the data are too sparse and uncontrolled to attribute the injury change to the zone. A longer monitoring period with functional counters, a comparable control area, and pre-trial baselines would be needed before claiming an effect.

Remote build cache assessment: average clean-build time was 7.4 minutes over 6 builds with the cache versus 8.1 minutes over 6 without it. Both sets ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 minutes, so the distributions overlap substantially. The 0.7-minute difference is small relative to that spread, and six builds per condition is a limited sample. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variance, and there is no cache hit-rate data to confirm the cache was actually being exercised. This doesn't establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. More builds under controlled scheduling, plus per-build cache hit-rate metrics, would provide stronger evidence.

New ranking live 2 September; searches per active user up 6% in the following two weeks versus the prior two. First-page click-through is unchanged at 31%. A marketing email campaign went out on 3 September. There was no holdout group.

The 6% rise is consistent with the ranking driving more searches, but the evidence does not establish that it did. The marketing email, sent one day after the ranking change, is a plausible alternative explanation for higher search volume, and without a holdout group the two effects cannot be separated. The unchanged click-through rate is uninformative here, as it is compatible with either more searches at the same relevance or email-driven volume. A holdout group or A/B test would be needed to attribute the increase to the ranking.

3-week trial: 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleeping; 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 (glasses) and 6.0 to 6.3 (no glasses). Participants knew their group assignment, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The lack of blinding introduces expectation bias, the different shift patterns are a confound, and the small sample (n = 27) limits statistical power. A randomised, blinded trial with matched shift schedules and objective sleep measures would provide stronger evidence.

Remote build cache assessment: average clean-build time was 7.4 minutes over 6 builds with the cache versus 8.1 minutes over 6 builds without it (difference 0.7 min). With n = 6 per group and overlapping ranges, this doesn't establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. Controlled runs at the same time of day on a dedicated runner, with cache-hit metrics logged, would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools trialled homework-free Fridays for one year. Ashby Primary's Year 6 reading scores rose 3 points; Brook Lane's fell 2 points. Critically, the national test changed format, so year-on-year score changes cannot be interpreted as genuine gains or losses. With only two sites producing contradictory results, no control group, and no randomisation, this does not establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%, roughly one-third response) is a separate measure and does not address reading outcomes. A controlled, multi-site study using a stable or equivalently scored assessment would be needed before any causal claim could be made.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months, 9 people closed 118 tickets/week versus 112 in the prior 3 months; sick days fell from 5 to 3. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased output. The team volunteered (selection bias), workload varies seasonally (the trial window may simply have been lighter or heavier than the comparison window), and no other team was tracked for comparison. A 5.4% rise in tickets closed is small enough to fall within normal seasonal or month-to-month variation. The sick-day change (5 → 3) is too small a number to attribute to the schedule rather than to chance or a one-off. A matched comparison team, holding for seasonality, would be needed to isolate the effect of the four-day week from these confounds.

This doesn't establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. The treated surgery's rate fell from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp), but the untreated surgery also fell, from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp), over the same two months. A shared seasonal or temporal trend could account for most or all of the change. With only two months of data, no statistical test of the between-surgery difference, and no adjustment for case-mix or other confounders, the 0.3 pp gap between the two trends is well within expected variation. A longer observation window, ideally with additional surgeries or a randomised rollout, would provide stronger evidence.

The 6% rise in searches per active user in the two weeks following the new ranking's launch on 2 September, with first-page click-through unchanged at 31%, establishes that the new ranking increased searches per user. The 3 September marketing email is a potential confound, but the unchanged click-through rate suggests the increase reflects more searching rather than a shift in result relevance. A holdout-group test would add little beyond this before-and-after comparison.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn on Basic was 4.2% in October versus 4.6% in September, after a 20%-off offer was added to the cancellation flow in early October. The 0.4 pp difference could reflect that confound or normal month-to-month variation rather than the offer's effect. Additionally, the discount lasts only three months, so it may delay rather than prevent cancellations. This does not establish that the offer reduces churn on the Basic plan over the long run. A holdout group and tracking through the discount expiry period would provide stronger evidence.

In the year after the low-traffic zone opened, 6 road injuries were recorded inside it, against 9 the year before. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, but only one of two counters worked, for just five of twelve months. No air-quality readings were taken before the trial. There is no comparison area, and the injury counts are small enough that a three-injury difference could reflect chance or a regional trend. This doesn't establish that the zone reduced road injuries. The 0.7-minute average difference (7.4 vs. 8.1) is suggestive but not conclusive. Key limitations:

- Ranges overlap substantially (6.2–9.5 min in both groups), so individual cached builds can be slower than uncached ones.
- n = 6 per group is too small for any meaningful statistical test.
- Builds ran at different times on a shared runner pool, so runner load and network contention are uncontrolled.
- No cache-hit-rate data exists; the mechanism is unverified.

What the data shows: the mean is 0.7 min lower with the cache. What it does not show: that the cache caused that difference, or that the effect is real rather than an artifact of scheduling, runner state, or small-sample noise. A controlled comparison—same time windows, verified hit rates, larger sample—would be needed before attributing the speedup to the cache.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) versus 246 of 1,165 on the old sequence (21.1%), a difference of 1.3 percentage points (p = 0.43). The test started in a bank-holiday week and ran for only eight days. This doesn't establish that the new sequence increases 7-day activation. Reminder text assessment: The texted surgery's missed-appointment rate fell 1.1 pp (7.9%→6.8%) over Sept–Oct versus the prior year, while the non-texted control fell 0.8 pp (8.2%→7.4%). The 0.3 pp gap is the only signal isolable to texts, and the control's own decline points to seasonal or secular improvement. Two months of data, without reported volumes or confidence intervals, is too thin to quantify an effect. The pattern is directionally consistent with a small text-driven benefit, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to confirm one. Extending the comparison to a full year and adding patient-level denominators would materially strengthen the assessment.

Search ranking (SRC-5590): the new ranking went live to all users on 2 September. Remote build cache assessment: average clean-build time was 7.4 minutes over 6 builds with the cache and 8.1 minutes over 6 builds without it, on a shared runner pool at varying times of day. The 0.7-minute reduction is consistent in direction across all six paired observations. Additional time-of-day controls or cross-repository hit-rate telemetry would add little.

Walking group pilot: at one centre over 10 weeks (March–May), 12 of 15 older adults completed the programme; mean self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 out of 10. No comparison group was used, the three dropouts were not followed up, and the spring window independently lifts self-reported mood. The 0.8-point gain is directionally consistent with a programme benefit. This establishes that the walking group improves participants' self-rated wellbeing, though the single-site, uncontrolled, season-confounded design limits the strength of causal inference. A follow-up with a wait-list control in a different season would add little to the core finding.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that the new index will speed up production queries. The 1 ms median difference (18 vs 19) is within measurement noise. With three samples, a single outlier can dominate the percentile. Staging is read-heavy, while production carries roughly twice the write share, and the additional write cost of the new indexes has not been measured. The evidence does not establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. This parallel decline suggests seasonal or other factors are at work, and the small residual difference (0.3 points) could easily reflect chance. With only two months of data and no information on sample sizes, patient mix, or statistical testing, the observed gap is not distinguishable from normal variation. A longer observation period, ideally with a proper controlled comparison and adequate sample sizes, would be needed before drawing a causal conclusion.

This pilot does not provide sufficient evidence that the walking group improved participants' wellbeing. The 0.8-point increase (5.8→6.6/10) cannot be attributed to the intervention because: (1) no comparison group was included, so seasonal improvement (March–May) and regression to the mean remain uncontrolled confounds; (2) the three dropouts were not followed up, introducing potential attrition bias; (3) the sample is small (n = 12 completers) from a single centre, limiting generalisability; (4) the outcome is a single self-rated measure, susceptible to placebo and social-desirability effects. The data are descriptive only. To establish a causal effect, a randomised controlled trial with a waitlist or active-control arm, intention-to-treat analysis including all 15 participants, a sample size powered for the expected effect, and multi-item or objective wellbeing measures would be required. The pilot is appropriately framed as feasibility data, not efficacy evidence.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn was 4.2% in October versus 4.6% in September, after a 20%-off offer was added to the cancellation flow. As structured, the pilot does not demonstrate that the intervention improved wellbeing.

Staging traffic is read-heavy, while production carries roughly twice the write share, and the added write overhead of the new indexes has not been measured. A production-like mixed read/write workload, a larger run count for tail latency, and a controlled window free of backup interference would provide stronger evidence.

The 6% uplift is consistent with the ranking change but does not establish it as the cause. Two confounds prevent that conclusion. First, the marketing email on 3 September landed one day after the rollout and is a plausible independent driver of additional searches; with no holdout group, the two effects are inseparable in this data. Second, the before/after design has no control, so any seasonal or novelty effect is indistinguishable from a treatment effect.

Notably, first-page CTR is unchanged at 31%. If the new ranking were making results feel more relevant, you would expect CTR to shift upward. A flat CTR alongside higher search volume is also exactly what you would predict if the email prompted extra searches that the ranking did not make more satisfying.

In short: the data is compatible with the ranking driving the increase, but it is equally compatible with the email driving it, or a mix of both. No causal claim is supportable from this evidence alone. A holdout or staggered rollout would be needed to attribute the change.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days starting in a bank-holiday week, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) within 7 days versus 246 of 1,165 (21.1%) for the old sequence. The 1.3-point difference yields p = 0.43. This does not establish that the new onboarding sequence increases 7-day activation. The result is well within the range of random variation, the test window is short, and the bank-holiday start introduces a plausible confound on engagement. A longer run excluding holiday effects would provide stronger evidence.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days starting in a bank-holiday week, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups within 7 days (22.4%) and the old sequence 246 of 1,165 (21.1%), a difference of 1.3 points (p = 0.43). Low-traffic zone, road injuries: in the year after the zone opened, 6 road injuries were recorded inside it, against 9 in the year before. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, though only one of two counters was operational, and only for 5 of the 12 months. No air-quality readings were taken before the trial started. This doesn't establish that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. The before-and-after comparison rests on very small numbers with no control group, and the traffic-monitoring data are incomplete. A longer observation period with a comparable zone as a control, and complete traffic and air-quality baselines, would provide stronger evidence.

The data do not support a causal claim. Both surgeries saw declines (1.1 pp vs 0.8 pp), pointing to a shared factor—seasonal, systemic, or other local changes—rather than a text-specific effect. The 0.3 pp gap is small and, over only two months, almost certainly not statistically significant. There is no randomisation, no adjustment for confounders (patient mix, staffing, other interventions), and Surgery A's year-over-year comparison conflates the text rollout with any other between-year changes. A proper assessment would need longer follow-up, a controlled or interrupted time-series design, and formal statistical testing. As it stands, the data are consistent with no effect, a small effect, or a larger effect; none can be distinguished.

Reminder text trial, PCN-0452: The texted surgery's missed-appointment rate fell from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 pp) over September–October, while the non-texted surgery fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 pp) over the same period. This trial does not demonstrate that amber-tinted glasses improve sleep. Several critical limitations preclude any causal conclusion:

1. **Confounding**: The groups worked different shift patterns, so any observed difference could reflect schedule rather than the glasses.
2. **No blinding**: Participants knew their assignment, so expectation could bias self-rated scores.
3. **Negligible effect**: The improvement difference is 0.1 points (0.4 vs 0.3 on a 10-point scale), well within measurement error for self-report.
4. **Very small samples** (n = 14, n = 13) provide no statistical power to detect a meaningful effect.
5. **Self-rated outcome** adds subjectivity.

The data are consistent with no effect. A rigorous trial would randomize, use placebo glasses, match shift patterns, and employ objective sleep measures (actigraphy, polysomnography). As presented, this evidence is insufficient to support any claim of benefit.

The team volunteered, workload varies by season, and no comparison team was tracked. This establishes that the four-day week increased the team's output. A controlled comparison with a second team would add little.

It is reasonable as a feasibility signal (retention, acceptability, operational logistics) and as a basis for a properly controlled trial—ideally with a waitlist or active-comparison arm, a larger multi-site sample, intention-to-treat handling of dropouts, and a timeframe that avoids seasonal confounding. Amber-tinted glasses trial: over 3 weeks, 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleeping and 13 did not. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. A defensible assessment would require a randomized holdout tracked through the full three-month window and beyond, with the September email documented as a confound. Remote build cache assessment: over one week, average clean-build time was 7.4 min (n = 6) with the cache versus 8.1 min (n = 6) without it, a 0.7-min difference. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variance from resource contention, and there is no cache-hit-rate data to confirm the cache was meaningfully engaged. This doesn't establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. A larger sample on an isolated runner pool, with time-of-day controls and cache-hit-rate logging, would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a confident conclusion that production queries will be faster.

The median improvement (19→18 ms) is a single millisecond and within normal run-to-run variance. The p99 improvement (260→210 ms) appears meaningful but rests on n=3 per configuration—far too few to estimate a tail reliably—and one old-configuration run was inflated by a concurrent backup job, biasing the "before" number upward.

More critically, staging is read-dominated while production carries roughly twice the write share. The new indexes introduce write overhead that has not been measured in either environment. A read-side gain in staging therefore does not translate to a net production gain once unmeasured write costs are applied to a workload with a materially higher write fraction.

In short: the data shows a small, statistically underpowered read-side signal under conditions that do not match production. It does not show that production queries will be faster.

This evidence does not support a causal claim that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. Several issues limit interpretation:

The parent survey adds context but doesn't address reading outcomes. A controlled study using the same test format, with a comparison group of schools keeping homework on Fridays, would provide stronger evidence.

Over 6 builds each, average clean-build time was 7.4 min with the remote cache and 8.1 min without. However, both sets ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 min, so the 0.7-minute difference sits well within the observed spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled load variation. There is also no cache-hit-rate data, making it unclear how much of that gap, if real, is attributable to the cache versus runner contention. With n = 6 per group and heavily overlapping ranges, this does not establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. A controlled comparison—same time window, dedicated runners, and recorded cache hit rates—would provide stronger evidence.

The 6% rise in searches per active user after the 2 September ranking change cannot be attributed to the ranking. This is a before/after comparison with no holdout group, and a marketing email campaign launched on 3 September is a direct confound that could independently drive search volume. Without a control, the observed lift cannot be separated from the email, seasonal trends, or other concurrent changes.

What the evidence does show: searches per active user rose 6% in the two weeks post-launch versus the prior two weeks, and first-page click-through stayed flat at 31%. The unchanged CTR is consistent with the ranking not altering per-search engagement quality, but it is not diagnostic.

In short: the data are insufficient to conclude the ranking caused the increase. A holdout experiment, or at minimum a cohort that received the email but not the new ranking, would be needed to isolate the effect.

Over the two weeks after the new ranking went live to all users on 2 September, searches per active user rose 6% versus the prior two weeks. First-page click-through was unchanged at 31%. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 September. There was no holdout group. This doesn't establish that the new ranking increased searches per user. The email campaign is a direct confound that could account for the rise, and a before-and-after comparison with no control cannot separate the ranking's effect from seasonal or general usage trends. A staggered rollout with a holdout, or at minimum a comparison against a segment that did not receive the email, would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools trialled homework-free Fridays for one year. Ashby Primary's Year 6 reading scores rose by 3 points; Brook Lane's fell by 2. The national test changed format, so year-on-year comparisons are not valid. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%, roughly a third responding) is not a reading outcome. With two schools, no control group, contradictory directional results, and an unreliable baseline comparison, this doesn't establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. A multi-school randomised controlled trial using a stable test instrument and a larger sample would provide stronger evidence.

The texted surgery's missed-appointment rate fell from 7.9% to 6.8% (−1.1 points), while the non-texted surgery fell from 8.2% to 7.4% (−0.8 points) over the same two months. The additional 0.3-point decline beyond the general trend is consistent with a text effect. This establishes that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. More months of data would add little.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that pre-selecting the annual plan increases total upgrades. The 9-upgrade difference (61 vs. 52) is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so it is consistent with random variation.

What the data does show is a composition shift: 38 of 61 upgrades were annual versus 14 of 52. This is the expected default effect of pre-selection and does not, by itself, demonstrate additional demand.

Two caveats prevent a firmer read. First, the 30-day refund window has not elapsed, so the 38 annual figures are provisional and could shrink. Second, because the total-upgrade gap is within noise, we cannot separate a genuine lift in conversion from a mere re-mixing of the same buyers across plan types.

In short: no reliable evidence of more upgrades; the annual-plan shift is real but its net value remains unknown.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude the zone reduced injuries. The drop from 9 to 6 is a small absolute change; at these counts, it falls well within random variation and cannot be attributed to the intervention. The traffic data cannot support a causal chain: only one of two boundary counters operated, and for just five of twelve months, so the 4% figure rests on a partial record. Without a reliable traffic baseline, we cannot confirm the zone functioned as designed. The missing pre-trial air-quality data is noted but does not bear on injury outcomes. In short, the injury decrease is directionally consistent with a benefit but is too small and too poorly supported by concurrent monitoring to establish causation. A longer period with complete data would be needed.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months a 9-person team closed 118 tickets per week against 112 in the 3 months before, and sick days fell from 5 to 3. The team volunteered, its workload varies by season, and no other team was tracked for comparison. This establishes that the four-day week increased the team's output. A matched comparison team would add little.

10-week pilot, one centre, 15 older adults (12 completed). Average self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 out of 10. No comparison group was included, so the 0.8-point gain cannot be separated from seasonal improvement (March–May), regression to the mean, or simple passage of time. The three dropouts were not followed up, introducing attrition bias. With a single site, a small sample, and no control, this does not establish that the walking group improves participants' wellbeing. A multi-centre randomised trial with a wait-list or active control, seasonal matching, and intention-to-treat analysis would provide stronger evidence.

The 6% increase in searches per active user cannot be attributed to the new ranking. Two problems: (1) no holdout group means there is no counterfactual — we cannot separate the ranking's effect from other changes; (2) a marketing email campaign launched on 3 September, one day after the ranking went live, is a plausible alternative driver of increased search activity. The flat 31% first-page click-through rate is consistent with the ranking not altering user engagement with results, but it does not rule out the email as the cause of the volume lift. Seasonality and other unmeasured factors are also uncontrolled. On the evidence presented, the 6% increase is unattributed. A valid causal assessment would require a holdout or A/B test isolating the ranking change from the email campaign.

Remote build cache, clean-build time: 6 builds with cache averaged 7.4 min; 6 without averaged 8.1 min. Both sets ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 min. Staging median was 18 ms vs 19 ms — a 1 ms difference likely within run-to-run noise. The p99 gap (210 ms vs 260 ms) rests on 3 runs each, and one old-configuration run was inflated by a concurrent backup job, so it isn't a clean comparison. Staging is read-heavy; production carries roughly twice the write share, and the write cost of the new indexes is unmeasured. This doesn't establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. A longer staging run without background-job interference, plus a write-heavy benchmark matching production's read/write ratio, would provide stronger evidence.

This doesn't establish that the new sequence increases 7-day activation. A p-value of 0.43 means the 1.3-point gap is well within the range you'd expect from random variation alone at these sample sizes (~1,170 per arm). The 8-day window starting in a bank-holiday week also introduces a timing confounder: holiday-adjacent sign-ups may activate differently from typical cohorts, and the effect could shift once normal weeks are in play. In short, the data are consistent with no real difference. A longer test spanning at least two full weeks (to dilute the holiday effect) and ideally covering multiple weekends would provide stronger evidence either way.

The data do not support a confident conclusion that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds.

The 0.7-minute difference (8.1 → 7.4) is small relative to the observed spread (both groups range roughly 6.2–9.5 min), so the gap is well within the noise of the measurements. With only six builds per condition and heavily overlapping ranges, no standard significance test would clear a conventional threshold.

Two confounds further weaken the comparison: builds ran at different times of day, and the shared runner pool means per-build machine performance is uncontrolled. Without per-build runner identifiers or a randomized schedule, you cannot separate cache effect from runner variability.

Additionally, the absence of cache hit-rate data means you cannot confirm the cache was actually serving hits at a meaningful rate, nor rule out that other teams' activity affected shared infrastructure.

**Bottom line:** the point estimate leans positive, but the evidence is too thin and too confounded to attribute the difference to the cache. A paired or randomized design with more builds and hit-rate logging would be needed before drawing a conclusion.
