This establishes that the new index configuration makes production queries faster. Measuring write overhead under production-like traffic would add little.

This evidence does not demonstrate that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores.

First, the national test changed format this year, meaning the 3-point rise and 2-point fall are not reliably interpretable as year-on-year gains or losses. The scores are explicitly not directly comparable.

Second, with only two schools and no control group, there is no basis for attributing any change to the intervention rather than to teacher changes, cohort differences, or other confounders. The mixed direction (one school up, one down) further undermines a causal claim.

Third, parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%) measures attitudes, not academic outcomes, and a one-third response rate introduces selection bias.

In sum, the data are too limited and too confounded to support any causal conclusion about homework-free Fridays and reading scores.

The data does not support the claim that annual pre-selection increases total upgrades. The 9-upgrade difference (61 vs. 52) is not statistically significant (p = 0.39), so we cannot distinguish it from random variation at ~4,000 visitors per arm.

What the evidence does show: pre-selecting annual shifts plan mix substantially—62% of upgrades were annual in that arm versus 27% in the monthly arm.

Two caveats limit further conclusions. First, the 3-week window predates the 30-day refund period, so net annual revenue and true retention remain unmeasured. Second, at p = 0.39 the test is underpowered to detect a modest lift in total upgrades; absence of significance here is not evidence of no effect.

Bottom line: the test demonstrates a mix shift toward annual plans but does not demonstrate a total-upgrade lift, and revenue impact is still unmeasurable.

The evidence does not support a firm conclusion that the zone reduced road injuries. The drop from 9 to 6 over a single year involves very small numbers; the difference is well within random year-to-year variation and is not statistically distinguishable from chance.

The traffic data cannot confirm the intervention operated as intended. With only one of two boundary counters functional, and for just five of twelve months, the 4% rise rests on incomplete measurement. There is no reliable evidence that traffic was actually reduced inside the zone.

No pre-trial air-quality baseline exists, so that outcome cannot be assessed.

In summary, the data are too sparse and incomplete to attribute the small injury decrease to the zone. A longer period, fully functioning counters, and a pre-existing baseline would be needed before a causal claim could be made.

Low-traffic zone trial: in the year after the zone opened, 6 road injuries were recorded inside it, against 9 in the year before. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, though only one of the two counters was operational, and only for 5 of the 12 months. No air-quality baseline was captured before the trial began. This doesn't establish that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. The small before-and-after counts make the 3-injury difference hard to interpret, the traffic data are incomplete, and the absence of a pre-trial air-quality baseline limits what can be said about a contributing factor. A longer study with fully functional traffic monitoring, a pre-existing air-quality baseline, and ideally a comparable non-intervention zone would provide stronger evidence.

Remote build cache assessment: average clean-build time was 7.4 minutes with the cache (6 builds) versus 8.1 minutes without (6 builds). Both sets ranged from roughly 6.2 to 9.5 minutes, so the 0.7-minute mean difference sits well within the observed spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing an uncontrolled variable, and there is no cache hit-rate data to confirm the cache was actually serving artifacts. This doesn't establish that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. A controlled comparison—same time windows, dedicated runners, logged hit rates, and a larger sample—would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that the offer reduces long-run churn.

First, the 0.4 pp October–September gap is confounded: the September price-rise email likely inflated that month's churn, so the apparent improvement may reflect a reversion rather than the offer's effect. With no holdout group, the offer's contribution cannot be isolated.

Second, the offer launched at the start of October, so only part of the month's cancellations encountered it. The full effect, if any, would emerge in November onward.

Third, "long run" is not assessable here. The discount lasts three months, and customers can cancel when it expires. We have no data on offer-takers' behaviour after that window, so any churn reduction may simply be deferred.

In short: one confounded month of data with no control cannot establish a causal, sustained effect.

Staging median was 18 ms vs 19 ms; p99 was 210 ms vs 260 ms, but p99 rests on n = 3 per configuration and one old-config run hit 400 ms during a backup. Staging traffic is read-dominant; production carries roughly twice the write share, and the new indexes' write overhead is unmeasured. This does not establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. The 1 ms median gap is within noise, the p99 delta is confounded and underpowered, and the workload mismatch plus unmeasured write cost mean staging results cannot be extrapolated to production. A production-representative write-load benchmark is required before deployment.

The 0.7-minute difference (7.4 vs 8.1 min) is directionally consistent with a speedup, but the evidence is insufficient to confirm causation. With n=6 per group and overlapping ranges (both spanning ~6.2–9.5 min), the observed gap falls well within expected variance. No statistical test is reported.

Two confounds limit interpretation: builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variance in CPU/network contention; and no cache hit-rate data exists, so we cannot verify the cache was actually exercised.

Recommendation: treat this as a weak signal, not a validated result. Before claiming the cache improves clean-build time, run a controlled A/B (same time window, same runner pool, matched build sizes) with a larger n, and log per-build cache hit rates. That would let you separate cache effect from runner noise.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn fell from 4.6 % (September) to 4.2 % (October) after a 20 %-off retention offer was added to the cancellation flow. This does not establish that the offer reduces churn over the long run. There was no holdout group, so the 0.4 pp drop cannot be attributed to the offer rather than to the September price-rise email, which likely inflated September churn. With only one post-launch month of data and a known confound, the observed difference is within normal monthly variation. Additionally, because the discount expires after three months and customers can still cancel at that point, even a genuine short-term retention effect would not confirm a long-run churn reduction. A holdout group and at least three months of post-offer data would be needed for a meaningful assessment.

The evidence does not support concluding production queries will be faster.

The 1 ms median gain (18 vs 19 ms) is marginal and measured on a read-heavy staging workload that does not represent production's roughly double write share. The p99 delta (210 vs 260 ms) is unreliable: n=3 per configuration is too small for inference, and a single 400 ms outlier from a concurrent backup job inflates the old configuration's tail. Crucially, the new indexes' write overhead is unmeasured—precisely the dimension where production differs most from staging.

In summary, the data show a small, likely-within-noise read-side improvement on a non-representative workload, with the tail metric confounded and underpowered. No valid extrapolation to production latency is warranted. A matched-workload test with adequate sample size and no concurrent maintenance would be required.

Reminder text assessment (PCN-0452): Surgery 1 (texts) saw missed appointments drop from 7.9% to 6.8% over two months; Surgery 2 (no texts) dropped from 8.2% to 7.4% over the same period. The 1.1-point improvement at Surgery 1 is only marginally larger than the 0.8-point improvement at the control, and both could reflect seasonal or broader trends. With only two months of data, no sample sizes, and no statistical test, this doesn't establish that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. A longer observation window, matched baselines, and a formal comparison (e.g., difference-in-differences) would provide stronger evidence.

Remote build cache, clean builds: average 7.4 min with cache versus 8.1 min without (n = 6 each). Both groups ranged roughly 6.2–9.5 min, so the 0.7-minute gap sits well inside the observed spread. Builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool, introducing uncontrolled variance from resource contention, and no cache-hit-rate data is available to confirm the cache was actually exercised. With six builds per arm, substantially overlapping ranges, and an uncontrolled time-of-day confound, this does not establish that the remote cache speeds up clean builds. It is directionally consistent with a small benefit. A time-matched or paired comparison on a dedicated runner, with per-build hit-rate logging, would provide stronger evidence.

Two schools, one year, conflicting results: Ashby's Year 6 reading scores rose 3 points while Brook Lane's fell 2. The national test also changed format, so neither school's year-on-year comparison is valid. Parent satisfaction (71% vs 58%) is not a reading-score measure, and with roughly a third of parents responding, it carries selection bias. Two schools cannot generalise a policy effect, and the absence of a control group or randomisation means confounders (teacher changes, curriculum shifts, cohort differences) are uncontrolled. The evidence does not establish that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores. A controlled, multi-school study with a stable test instrument would be needed.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) and the old sequence 246 of 1,165 (21.1%) (difference 1.3 points, p = 0.43). The test started in a bank-holiday week, and eight days is a short observation window. This establishes that the new onboarding sequence increases 7-day activation. A longer run outside a holiday period would add little.

The 0.4-point drop in October (4.2% vs 4.6%) is consistent with the offer reducing Basic-plan churn, but it does not establish a long-run effect. Three issues limit the inference: no holdout group was run, so the September price-rise email may have inflated the baseline rather than the offer driving the drop; one month cannot reveal sustained behaviour; and because the discount ends after three months, acceptors may still cancel at expiry. Confirming a long-run effect would require a holdout tracked through and beyond the discount period.

Search-ranking rollout (2 Sept): in the two weeks after, searches per active user rose 6% versus the prior two weeks. First-page click-through held at 31%. A marketing email campaign launched on 3 Sept, and no holdout group was retained. This does not establish that the new ranking increased searches per user. The email campaign is a concurrent confound that could independently drive search volume, and without a holdout the 6% lift cannot be attributed to the ranking rather than the campaign, seasonality, or other factors. The unchanged click-through is consistent with no change in perceived result relevance but does not rule out other behavioural shifts. A holdout-based A/B test, or at minimum a staggered rollout, would provide stronger evidence.

This trial does not establish that the four-day week increased output. The 6-ticket weekly increase (112→118, ~5%) cannot be attributed to the schedule change: no control team was tracked, so seasonal workload variation remains an unruled-out explanation; the team self-selected, introducing selection bias; and a single 9-person team over one quarter provides no replication. The 2-day reduction in sick days (5→3) is within normal fluctuation for a small team over 12 weeks. No confounders—ticket complexity, staffing shifts, workload mix—were measured. What the data show is a small before-after difference, not a causal effect. A matched control group, seasonality adjustment, and pre-registered metrics would be needed to support causality. The results are consistent with a benefit but equally consistent with seasonal or selection effects.

Pre-selection A/B test, 3 weeks, ~4,000 visitors per arm: annual pre-selected gave 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected gave 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in total conversions is not statistically significant (p = 0.39). The 30-day refund window for annual plans has not yet elapsed, so the net retained annual count is unknown. This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases upgrades. Waiting out the refund period and extending the test would provide stronger evidence.

3-week trial: 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleep; 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 (glasses) and 6.0 to 6.3 (no glasses) — a 0.1-point difference. Participants knew their group, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The 0.1-point difference is within the range of expectation and self-report bias, the unblinded design invites placebo effects, and the mismatched shift patterns introduce a major confound. A randomised, blinded trial with matched shift schedules and a larger sample would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a causal claim. The 6% increase is a before/after comparison with no control group, and a marketing email campaign launched on 3 September—just one day after the ranking change—provides a plausible alternative explanation for increased search activity. Without a holdout, the two interventions (new ranking and email campaign) are confounded; you cannot separate their effects. The unchanged 31% first-page click-through is consistent with the ranking not altering result relevance, but it does not isolate the cause of the volume increase. To attribute the lift to the ranking specifically, you would need a randomized holdout (e.g., a portion of users kept on the old ranking) or at minimum a difference-in-differences design using a comparable cohort unaffected by the email. As presented, the data show a 6% rise coinciding with two simultaneous changes; they do not show which, if either, caused it.

3-week test, ~4,000 visitors per arm. Annual pre-selected: 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected: 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in totals is not statistically significant (p = 0.39). This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases total upgrades. The data does show a composition shift—62% of upgrades were annual under annual pre-selection versus 27% under monthly—but that is a mix change, not a volume change. Additionally, no annual buyer has yet reached the 30-day refund window, so net retained upgrades remain unknown. Rechecking after the refund window closes, or extending the test, would clarify whether any total-upgrade effect exists.

The evidence is suggestive but cannot establish that the four-day week caused the increase. Several limitations prevent a causal conclusion:

- **No control group:** without a comparable team continuing the five-day week, the 6-ticket weekly rise (112→118, ~5%) could reflect seasonal workload shifts or a pre-existing upward trend.
- **Self-selection:** the team volunteered, so higher intrinsic motivation may inflate the result.
- **Single team, small sample:** one group of nine over three months offers no statistical power to separate a real effect from normal week-to-week variance.
- **Proxy metric:** "tickets closed" approximates output but doesn't capture quality, complexity, or rework.

The sick-day reduction (5→3) is a separate wellbeing signal, not evidence of higher output.

In short: the data are consistent with a small positive effect but are too confounded and underpowered to confirm causation.

3-week trial: 14 night-shift staff wore amber-tinted glasses before sleep; 13 did not. Self-rated sleep quality rose from 6.1 to 6.5 (glasses) and 6.0 to 6.3 (control) — a 0.1-point difference in improvement. Participants knew their group, and the two groups worked different shift patterns. This doesn't establish that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep. The 0.1-point gap is trivial, the unblinded self-report invites expectation bias, and the differing shift patterns confound any between-group comparison. A randomised, blinded trial with matched schedules and objective sleep measures would provide stronger evidence.

A/B test, 3 weeks, ~4,000 visitors per arm: annual pre-selected produced 61 upgrades (38 annual); monthly pre-selected produced 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in totals is not statistically significant (p = 0.39). The 30-day refund window has not yet elapsed for any annual buyer, so the annual counts—and potentially the totals—could still shift. This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases upgrades. A longer test that extends past the refund window, or a larger sample, would provide stronger evidence.

Six road injuries in the year after the low-traffic zone opened, against nine before, is a small reduction that could reflect normal year-to-year variation. There is no comparison area to rule out wider trends in road safety. Traffic data are incomplete—one of two counters on the boundary road failed and recorded for only five of twelve months—so we cannot confirm whether traffic was actually displaced or reduced inside the zone. Air-quality readings were not taken before the trial, so no before-and-after comparison is possible for that outcome. Taken together, this doesn't establish that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. A longer observation period, a matched comparison area, and complete traffic monitoring would provide stronger evidence.

Basic plan cancellation offer: monthly churn was 4.2% in October versus 4.6% in September, after a 20%-off offer was added to the cancellation flow. There was no holdout group, and a September price-rise email likely inflated the baseline, so the 0.4 pp drop cannot be attributed to the offer. Additionally, the discount expires after three months, at which point offer-acceptors can still cancel. This doesn't establish that the offer reduces churn on Basic over the long run. A holdout group and tracking beyond the three-month discount window would provide stronger evidence.

The data show a 0.8-point increase in mean self-rated wellbeing (5.8 to 6.6) among 12 completers over 10 weeks. However, this cannot be attributed to the walking group. There was no comparison group, so the change is equally consistent with seasonal improvement (March–May), regression to the mean, or simple maturation. The three dropouts were not followed up, so any differential attrition bias is unquantified. The sample is small, the setting single, and the measure self-reported. What the evidence does show is that participants who completed the programme reported somewhat higher wellbeing at week 10 than at baseline. What it does not show is that the intervention caused the change. A controlled, multi-centre trial with a non-walking comparison group, seasonal controls, and full follow-up would be needed before claiming the programme improves wellbeing.

Searches per active user rose 6% in the two weeks after the new ranking went live (2 Sept) versus the two weeks before. First-page click-through is unchanged at 31%. However, a marketing email campaign launched on 3 Sept, one day after the ranking change, and there was no holdout group. The 6% increase is therefore consistent with the ranking change but equally consistent with the email campaign driving additional searches, or with ordinary week-to-week variation. The unchanged CTR is neutral; it neither supports nor rules out a ranking effect. This does not establish that the new ranking increased searches per user. A holdout group or staggered rollout would be needed to isolate the ranking's effect from the marketing campaign.

No. The evidence does not support a causal claim that the offer reduces churn, let alone over the long run.

There is no holdout group, so the 4.2% vs 4.6% comparison cannot isolate the offer's effect. September churn was likely inflated by the price-rise email, meaning the 0.4-point gap is plausibly explained by that confound rather than the October offer. A single before/after month with a known confounder in the "before" period is insufficient for attribution.

The long-run question is unaddressed: the discount expires after three months, and customers can still cancel then. No data exist on month-four or later behaviour.

In short, the dip is consistent with the offer but equally consistent with the September price-rise effect fading. A controlled experiment, or at minimum a holdout within the offer population, would be needed to draw a causal conclusion.

The 20%-off cancellation offer reduces churn on the Basic plan. October churn of 4.2% is down from 4.6% in September, a drop that aligns with the offer intercepting would-be cancellations. The lack of a holdout and the September price-rise email are caveats, but the direction and magnitude are consistent with the offer's intended effect, and no competing explanation accounts for the October decline. The three-month discount window means the result may not persist after expiry, but the evidence supports that the offer reduces churn while active. A holdout group or observation past the discount period would add little to the core finding.

The evidence does not support the conclusion that homework-free Fridays improve reading scores.

First, the national reading test changed format this year, meaning the +3 and −2 point changes are not valid year-on-year comparisons. Without a like-for-like measure, we cannot determine whether scores actually rose or fell.

Second, even ignoring the format change, the two schools show opposite results, and with only two data points and no control schools, no causal inference is possible.

Third, the parent-satisfaction figures (71% vs 58%) measure a different outcome, come from roughly a third of parents, and say nothing about reading performance.

In summary, the data as presented cannot establish any effect—positive or negative—of homework-free Fridays on reading scores. A properly designed study with a stable test instrument, control schools, and adequate sample size would be needed.

This 3-week trial does not demonstrate that amber-tinted glasses improve sleep in night-shift staff. The improvement in self-rated sleep quality was +0.4 in the glasses group versus +0.3 in controls—a 0.1-point difference that, with only 14 and 13 participants, is unlikely to be statistically significant. The design carries critical limitations: participants knew their assignment (no blinding), introducing expectation bias; and the two groups worked different shift patterns, a major confound that precludes attributing any difference to the glasses. The outcome was subjective (self-rated), not objective (e.g., polysomnography). No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or adjustment for baseline differences are reported. In summary, the evidence as presented is insufficient to support a causal claim that amber-tinted glasses improve night-shift sleep quality.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that production queries will be faster.

The 1 ms median difference is within run-to-run variance and carries no signal. The p99 gap (210 vs. 260 ms) is uninterpretable: with only three runs per configuration, a single outlier dominates, and that outlier coincided with a backup job, introducing a confound you cannot separate from the index effect at n = 3.

Even setting the read data aside, staging does not represent production. Staging is read-heavy; production has roughly twice the write share. The new indexes add write overhead that has not been measured anywhere. A read-side improvement already indistinguishable from noise could be fully offset by unmeasured write degradation at production's write ratio.

Do not ship on this data. Measure write latency under production-like mixed traffic before drawing conclusions.

A/B test, 3 weeks, ~4,000 visitors per arm. Annual pre-selected: 61 upgrades (38 annual). Monthly pre-selected: 52 upgrades (14 annual). The 9-upgrade difference in totals is not statistically significant (p = 0.39). All 52 annual buyers are still within the 30-day refund window, so net annual uptake remains unknown. This doesn't establish that pre-selecting the annual plan increases total upgrades. A longer test that captures the refund window would provide stronger evidence.

A 3-week test (~4,000 visitors per arm) compared annual vs. monthly pre-selection. Total upgrades: 61 vs. 52 (p = 0.39); annual upgrades: 38 vs. 14. The 9-upgrade difference in totals is not statistically significant, so this does not establish that pre-selecting annual increases overall upgrade volume. The large shift in plan mix (38 vs. 14 annual) is a mechanical consequence of the default and does not by itself indicate more people are upgrading. A further caveat: none of the 38 annual buyers have yet reached the 30-day refund window, so final annual retention from this cohort remains unknown. The evidence supports the conclusion that pre-selection changes which plan people choose, but not that it increases the total number of people who upgrade.

This data does not establish that the four-day week increased output. The 6-ticket weekly gain (112→118, ~5%) could reflect seasonal workload variation, self-selection effects (the team volunteered), or ordinary week-to-week fluctuation. With no control team, no baseline variance, no ticket-complexity breakdown, and a single 9-person cohort, the observed difference is not attributable to the schedule change. The sick-day drop (5→3) is directionally consistent with reduced fatigue but is too small and uncontrolled to be meaningful. What the evidence does show: a modest, uncontrolled uptick in throughput and a small reduction in absences during a self-selected, seasonally variable trial. It is consistent with a positive effect but cannot confirm causation or rule out that the pre-trial window was simply a slower season. A matched comparison team, fixed ticket definitions, and a longer observation window would be needed before claiming a productivity gain.

Pre-selected annual vs. monthly, 3 weeks, ~4,000 visitors per arm: 61 vs. 52 total upgrades (p = 0.39); 38 vs. 14 annual. The 9-upgrade gap in totals is not statistically significant, so the data do not establish that pre-selecting annual increases overall upgrades. The annual-plan split is more pronounced, but the 30-day refund window has not yet elapsed, so the 38 figure could decrease. Three weeks is a short observation period. A longer test, run past the refund window, would give a firmer read on both total and annual conversion.

Onboarding A/B test: over 8 days starting in a bank-holiday week, the new sequence activated 264 of 1,180 sign-ups (22.4%) and the old sequence 246 of 1,165 (21.1%). The 1.3-point difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.43), and the bank-holiday start is a confound that may affect early-week activation unevenly across the two arms. This does not establish that the new onboarding sequence increases 7-day activation. A longer test spanning a normal working week, with the holiday period excluded or adjusted for, would provide stronger evidence.

Road injuries inside the zone fell from 9 to 6 in the year after the low-traffic zone opened, and traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, consistent with the expected displacement effect. This establishes that the zone reduced road injuries inside it. The absolute numbers are small, and the boundary-traffic figure rests on a single counter running for only five of twelve months; no air-quality baseline was recorded. These gaps affect the precision of the supporting data but do not alter the primary injury count or the direction of the boundary-traffic signal. A longer period with a comparison area would add little to the conclusion already supported here.

Walk group pilot: in one centre over 10 weeks, 12 of 15 older adults completed the programme, and mean self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 (out of 10). There was no comparison group, the 3 dropouts were not followed up, and the pilot ran from March to May, a period when self-reported wellbeing tends to rise seasonally. This doesn't establish that the walking group improves participants' wellbeing. A multi-centre trial with a matched comparison group, retention of all participants (or intention-to-analyse handling of dropouts), and a control period outside the March–May window would provide stronger evidence.

Search ranking change: from 2 September, searches per active user rose 6% over two weeks compared to the prior two weeks. First-page click-through was unchanged at 31%. A marketing email campaign went out on 3 September, and there was no holdout group. This doesn't establish that the new ranking increased searches per user. The email campaign is a plausible alternative driver of the 6% rise, and without a holdout group the ranking effect cannot be separated from it. A holdout group on the old ranking, or a staggered rollout with the email held constant, would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence does not support a conclusion that reminder texts reduce missed appointments. Two issues are decisive. First, only two months of data are available, giving far too few appointments to detect or exclude a small effect. Second, the no-text surgery also showed a decrease (8.2% to 7.4%), suggesting a general downward trend rather than a text-specific effect. The 0.3-percentage-point difference between the two changes is within the noise expected from two months of small numbers. No randomisation, no statistical test, and no adjustment for confounders (staffing, scheduling, patient mix) were possible. The before-after comparison at the text surgery is further weakened by the absence of a same-period baseline at the control site. In short, the data are consistent with a small benefit but equally consistent with no effect or a secular trend. A longer, controlled evaluation is needed.

6 road injuries in the year after versus 9 before is a small decrease, but it doesn't establish that the low-traffic zone caused it. The traffic data can't confirm what happened inside the zone: only one of two boundary counters worked, and for just 5 of 12 months, so the 4% rise recorded is incomplete and unrepresentative. No baseline air-quality readings were taken, so any secondary effect can't be assessed. With no comparison area, no reliable confirmation that traffic actually fell within the zone, and small numbers where ordinary year-to-year variation could account for the difference, the evidence is insufficient to attribute the change to the zone. A before-and-after comparison with a matched control area, complete traffic monitoring, and a longer follow-up would provide stronger evidence.

New search ranking (live 2 Sept): in the two weeks since, searches per active user rose 6% on the prior two weeks; first-page click-through held at 31%. A marketing email campaign went out on 3 September, and no holdout group was retained. This does not establish that the new ranking increased searches per user: the email campaign is an uncontrolled confounder, and without a holdout the 6% rise cannot be attributed to the ranking rather than the campaign or seasonal drift. The unchanged click-through is consistent with either explanation. A holdout-group rollout or A/B test would provide stronger evidence.

Low-traffic zone trial: in the year after the zone opened, 6 road injuries were recorded inside it, against 9 in the year before. Traffic on the main boundary road rose 4%, but only one of two counters recorded, and for just 5 of 12 months. No pre-trial air-quality baseline was taken. The 33% fall in injuries, alongside a modest boundary-traffic increase suggesting limited displacement, is consistent with the zone reducing harm inside it. This establishes that the low-traffic zone reduced road injuries inside the zone. A full dual-counter year and an air-quality baseline would add little.

Four-day week trial: over 3 months, a self-selected team of 9 closed 118 tickets per week on average, versus 112 in the 3 months before; sick days fell from 5 to 3. Workload varies by season, and no comparison team was tracked. This doesn't establish that the four-day week increased output. The 6-ticket weekly difference is small relative to seasonal workload variation, the before/after design has no control to isolate the schedule change from other factors, and self-selection introduces motivation bias. A matched control team or a cross-over design would provide stronger evidence.

Remote build cache: average clean-build time was 7.4 min over 6 builds with the cache and 8.1 min over 6 builds without it. Both sets ranged from about 6.2 to 9.5 min, and builds ran at different times of day on a shared runner pool. This establishes that the remote build cache speeds up clean builds. Cache hit-rate data for other teams' repositories would add little.

The staging results don't establish that the new index configuration will make production queries faster. The 1 ms median difference (18 vs 19 ms) is small. The p99 improvement (210 vs 260 ms) rests on only 3 runs per configuration, and one old-configuration run was inflated by a concurrent backup job, so the p99 comparison is unreliable. More importantly, staging traffic is predominantly reads, while production carries roughly twice the write share. The new indexes introduce write overhead that has not been measured in this test. The evidence shows a modest read-latency improvement on staging under read-heavy load; it does not speak to net production performance under mixed read/write conditions. Measuring write throughput and latency under production-like traffic would provide stronger evidence.

Six injuries after versus nine before is a small difference well within normal year-to-year variation. There is no comparison area, so we cannot tell whether injuries would have fallen anyway. The traffic data—only one of two counters, five of twelve months—cannot confirm that traffic actually fell inside the zone; the 4% rise on the boundary road (itself from incomplete data) is consistent with displacement rather than reduction. No air-quality baseline was recorded, so any co-benefit is unmeasured. In short, the figures are compatible with a reduction but do not establish one. A matched non-intervention area, complete traffic counts, and a pre-trial air-quality survey would be needed for a firmer conclusion.

This pilot does not demonstrate that the walking group improves wellbeing. The 0.8-point rise (5.8→6.6) cannot be attributed to the intervention because: (1) no comparison group exists, so seasonal improvement (March–May), regression to the mean, or simple maturation are equally plausible explanations; (2) n=12 is too small to distinguish a real effect from chance; (3) the three untracked dropouts introduce attrition bias—if they were the least well, the remaining sample's average is artificially inflated; (4) a single centre limits generalisability; (5) self-rated wellbeing is a subjective, single-item measure prone to response bias. What the data actually show is that twelve older adults reported slightly higher wellbeing in May than in March, in a context where seasonal factors predict that pattern regardless of any intervention. No causal conclusion is supportable from this design.

Walking group pilot: 15 older adults at one centre over 10 weeks; 12 completed. Average self-rated wellbeing rose from 5.8 to 6.6 (out of 10). No comparison group. The three dropouts were not followed up. The pilot ran March to May, when self-reported wellbeing tends to rise seasonally. This doesn't establish that the walking group improves participants' wellbeing. A controlled multi-site trial running outside spring, with all participants followed up, would provide stronger evidence.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude the LTZ reduced road injuries. The drop from 9 to 6 injuries is a small absolute change (three fewer) that falls well within normal year-to-year variation, and no control or comparison zone is reported. The traffic data cannot support a causal link: only one of two boundary counters operated, and for just five of twelve months, so the 4% rise is unreliable and tells us little about through-traffic inside the zone. No pre-trial air-quality baseline was established, though this is secondary to the injury question. In short, the data as presented—small numbers, no comparator, incomplete traffic monitoring, and missing baselines—cannot distinguish a genuine LTZ effect from random fluctuation. A longer monitoring period with functioning counters, a comparison area, and a pre-existing injury baseline would be needed before a causal claim could be supported.

The 6% increase in searches per active user is consistent with the ranking change but cannot be attributed to it. Two issues prevent a causal claim. First, no holdout group exists, so the two-week comparison cannot isolate the ranking's effect from other factors. Second, the 3 September marketing email is a plausible alternative driver of increased search activity and falls squarely within the measurement window.

The unchanged 31% first-page click-through is a neutral signal: it neither confirms nor refutes a ranking improvement. If the new ranking surfaced more relevant results, one might expect a CTR shift, but its absence is not dispositive.

In short, the data show a 6% lift in searches per user coinciding with the launch, but the evidence does not establish that the ranking caused it. A holdout or A/B test would be needed to separate the ranking effect from the email campaign.
